questions.q: Under Section 2(a) of the Indian Contract Act, a 'proposal' is defined as when a person signifies willingness to do or abstain from an act:
o: Only to obtain payment
With a view to obtaining the assent of the other to such act or abstinence
Only in writing
Only through a lawyer

questions.q: A shopkeeper displaying goods with price tags in a shop window is generally treated as:
o: A binding offer to sell
An invitation to offer, not an offer itself
A completed contract with any customer who enters
An acceptance
questions.src: Settled contract law principle — display of goods is an invitation to treat, not itself an offer

questions.q: In Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. (1892), the court held that a general offer to the public:
o: Can never be legally binding
Can be accepted by any person who performs the stated conditions with knowledge of the offer
Requires separate written communication of acceptance in every case
Applies only to written advertisements, not verbal ones
questions.src: Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. (Court of Appeal, 1892)

questions.q: In Lalman Shukla v. Gauri Dutt (1913), the claimant's reward claim failed because:
o: He did not actually find the missing boy
He performed the act without knowledge of the reward offer, so there was no valid acceptance
The reward was never publicly announced at all
He was a minor at the time
questions.src: Lalman Shukla v. Gauri Dutt (Allahabad HC, 1913) — offer must be communicated and known to the acceptor

questions.q: A counter-offer made in response to an original offer has the legal effect of:
o: Automatically accepting the original offer
Destroying the original offer, which can no longer later be accepted
Extending the original offer's validity period
Having no legal effect on the original offer
questions.src: Hyde v. Wrench (1840) — a counter-offer destroys the original offer

questions.q: Under Section 5 of the Indian Contract Act, a proposal may generally be revoked:
o: At any time, even after a valid contract is formed
At any time before the communication of acceptance is complete against the proposer
Only with the other party's written consent
Never, once made

questions.q: Under Section 2(d) of the Indian Contract Act, consideration may move from:
o: Only the promisee
Only the promisor
The promisee or any other person
Only a government authority
questions.src: Indian Contract Act 1872, Section 2(d) — broader than the strict English rule requiring consideration only from the promisee

questions.q: In Chinnaya v. Ramayya (1882), the court held the aunt could enforce the annuity promise even though she gave no consideration herself, because:
o: The daughter had signed a separate written contract with the aunt
Consideration had moved from the mother (a third party) to the daughter, which Indian law permits
Family agreements are automatically enforceable regardless of consideration
The aunt was a minor

questions.q: Under Section 25, which of the following is a recognised statutory exception to 'no consideration, no contract'?
o: Any oral promise between strangers
A written, registered promise based on natural love and affection between near relations
A verbal promise made in anger
A promise made under duress

questions.q: The Doctrine of Privity of Contract generally means:
o: Any person can sue on any contract, whether or not they are a party to it
Only parties to a contract can sue and be sued on it — a stranger to the contract generally cannot enforce it
Contracts are automatically enforceable by the government
Privity has no legal significance in Indian contract law
questions.src: Settled contract law principle, illustrated in Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Co v Selfridge & Co (1915)

questions.q: Under Indian law, an agreement made by a minor is:
o: Voidable at the minor's option
Fully valid and enforceable like any adult contract
Void ab initio — void from the very beginning
Valid only if a guardian co-signs
questions.src: Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (Privy Council, 1903)

questions.q: Following Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose, if a minor fraudulently misrepresents their age to obtain a loan, the lender generally:
o: Can fully enforce the contract due to the minor's fraud
Cannot recover the amount, since no valid contract existed and no estoppel operates against a minor
Can have the minor imprisoned
Can force the minor's parents to pay in all circumstances
questions.src: Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (Privy Council, 1903) — no estoppel against a minor

questions.q: Under Section 68, if necessaries suited to a minor's condition in life are supplied to them, the supplier is entitled to reimbursement from:
o: The minor personally, as an ordinary contractual debt
The minor's property only, not as a personal contractual liability
The minor's school or guardian only, never the minor
No one — there is no remedy at all

questions.q: A person of unsound mind can validly enter into a contract:
o: Never, under any circumstances
During lucid intervals, when they are capable of understanding the contract and forming a rational judgment
Only if a court explicitly permits it in advance for every transaction
Only for contracts below a specified monetary value
questions.src: Settled contract law principle on capacity — persons of unsound mind can contract during lucid intervals

questions.q: Under Section 15, 'Coercion' is defined in terms of:
o: Using a dominant position to influence someone's will
Committing or threatening to commit an act forbidden by the IPC, or unlawfully detaining/threatening to detain property
Making an innocent false statement
A mutual mistake of fact

questions.q: The key distinguishing feature between Fraud (Section 17) and Misrepresentation (Section 18) is:
o: Fraud must always be in writing
Fraud involves intent to deceive or reckless disregard for truth; misrepresentation is an innocent, honest (though mistaken) belief
Misrepresentation always leads to criminal liability
There is no real legal difference between the two

questions.q: A bilateral mistake of fact essential to an agreement, under Section 20, renders the agreement:
o: Voidable at the option of either party
Void
Fully valid, since mistakes don't affect contract validity
Automatically illegal

questions.q: Under Section 23, an agreement's object or consideration is unlawful (making the agreement void) if it is:
o: Merely inconvenient to one party
Forbidden by law, fraudulent, injurious to person/property, or opposed to public policy
Simply unusual or unconventional
Made on a public holiday

questions.q: 'Novation' as a mode of discharge of contract refers to:
o: Cancelling a contract with no substitute at all
Substituting a new contract for an existing one, either between the same parties on new terms or with a new party
A unilateral declaration ending a contract without the other party's consent
A court order that always terminates the contract
questions.src: Settled contract law principle on discharge by agreement

questions.q: The Doctrine of Frustration under Section 56 applies when:
o: A party simply changes their mind about performing
Performance becomes impossible or unlawful due to an event occurring after the contract was made, which the promisor could not prevent
One party becomes slightly less profitable than expected
The contract was impossible to perform from the very outset

questions.q: In Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co (1954), the Supreme Court held that Section 56's 'impossibility':
o: Means only strict, literal physical impossibility
Extends to situations where the very foundation of the contract is destroyed, making performance impracticable
Never applies to any Indian contract
Applies exclusively to government contracts
questions.src: Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co (Supreme Court, 1954)

questions.q: 'Anticipatory breach' of contract occurs when:
o: A party fails to perform exactly on the due date
A party declares, before the due date, an intention not to perform their obligations
Both parties mutually agree to cancel the contract
The contract becomes frustrated by an external event
questions.src: Settled contract law principle on anticipatory breach

questions.q: Under Hadley v. Baxendale (1854), damages for breach of contract are recoverable if they:
o: Arise naturally from the breach, OR were reasonably in the contemplation of both parties at the time of contracting
Are of any kind whatsoever, however remote or unforeseeable
Only involve direct physical property damage
Were caused entirely by an unrelated third party

questions.q: 'Liquidated damages' under Section 74 refer to a sum that is:
o: Designed purely to punish the breaching party, unrelated to actual loss
A genuine pre-estimate of the loss likely to result from breach, agreed in advance by the parties
Only awarded in criminal proceedings
Never enforceable under Indian law

questions.q: Under Section 70, if a person lawfully does something for another non-gratuitously and the other person enjoys the benefit, the person who benefited is:
o: Never liable to compensate, since there was no express contract
Bound to make compensation, or to restore the thing so delivered
Liable only if there is a signed written agreement
Liable only in criminal proceedings
